## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Bāhiyajātaka* (Ja 108) is a story belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. Its opening narrative is set while the Buddha was dwelling in the Gabled Chamber (*Kūṭāgārasālā*) at the Great Grove near Vesālī [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The occasion relates to a faithful Licchavi prince who embraced the Teaching and extended generous hospitality to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, despite the prince's wife being excessively corpulent and poorly attired [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
The tale's canonical stanza begins with the incipit *Sikkheyya sikkhitabbāni* ("Learn thou betimes" / verse 467) [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. In the associated story of the past, a woman is seen discreetly easing herself in public; her modest demeanor so impresses the king that he chooses her as his wife [Anandajoti 2010]. In the narrative's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the married couple of the past with the Licchavi husband and wife, identifying himself as the wise minister (*paṇḍitāmacco*) who counseled the king [Fausböll 1877].
Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any external parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan literature, and DharmaNexus identifies no significant Pali-internal text reuse [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the text in four modern languages [SuttaCentral].
